generatedProse.concept-context: In academic study, whatever your subject, an essay is expected to argue, not just describe. A question that asks you to assess or evaluate wants a reasoned position, built from the evidence and shaped by the relevant reading. The argument is carried by structure: the introduction states what you will argue, each body paragraph makes one point supported by evidence, and the conclusion draws the case together. Writing that holds a line of argument across its parts is valued in every discipline.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing the introduction to an essay on the same question.

Student A opens with two broad sentences about why the topic matters, then lists what the essay will cover. It reads smoothly, but it never says what the writer will argue. The reader reaches the body with no sense of a position, so each point arrives on its own rather than as a step in a case. This is structure without an argument.

Student B introduces the topic, notes briefly how the reading tends to treat it, and ends with a clear line of argument: what will be argued, and why. Now the body has something to carry. Each paragraph makes one point that advances the argument, and the reader can follow the case building. This is structure doing its job.

Both introductions are well written. Only Student B used the structure to set up an argument the rest of the essay could carry.
generatedProse.summary: An argumentative essay, in any subject, is a continuous response built around one argument, and that argument is carried by structure. The introduction states the line of argument, the body makes one point per paragraph, and the conclusion brings them together. You can now recognise the argument in each part and say what a strong introduction must do. The next lesson shows how sources are woven in to support it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's introduction stronger than Student A's?

items.text: It ended with a clear line of argument, so the body had a case to carry.
It was longer and used more technical terms.
It listed everything the essay would cover.
It avoided mentioning the relevant reading.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B stated a line of argument, so each paragraph could advance it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what let Student B's body build a case rather than offer separate points.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's introduction ended with a clear line of argument. Student A's listed topics and stated no case.
